newsitem.title: USA: U.S. has no plans to cut Albania aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. has no plans to cut Albania aid.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday accused Albania of intimidating opposition politicians and shutting down the Albanian press, but said it would not be in Washington's interest to end aid.

"We regret very much that the Albanian authorities are using the state of emergency to intimidate opposition politicians and to shut down the Albanian press and to shut down Voice of America," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said referring to the U.S.-funded radio network that broadcasts overseas.

"Now, it's incumbent upon the Albanian government, if it believes itself to be a democracy, to allow international broadcast stations like VOA to broadcast freely and in an unfettered way into Albania. We also think it's a great mistake to suspend the rights of journalists, foreign or domestic, in Albania itself," he said.

The New York Times, in an editorial in Tuesday's editions, argued that "with Albania reaching a flash point, American and Western assistance should be suspended until the (President Sali) Berisha government starts moving from repression toward potlical conciliation."
But Burns said such a move would not be in U.S. self-interest.

The $27 million in 1997 assistance for Albania is not directed toward the government "but towards non-governmental organisations, with an emphasis on democratization, on the rule of law, on free market economics, on helping people -- helping independent journalists, for instance," he said.

"All of that money is directed to building a democracy in Albania. And surely, when democracy is threatened by the government and by the military, that's not the time to withdraw your support from the grassroots political activists who do stand for democracy, or from journalists who want to write and broadcast what they are seeing," he said.

Burns said there was a limit to what the United States could do to help quell the crisis in Albania beyond bonding with neighbouring countries like Italy and Greece to pressure Tirana to resolve the situation peacefully and democratically.

He said an effort was being made to have the United States and the Europeans, possibly in the Organisation on Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), adopt a unified position on Albania. He did not know if OSCE would send a mission Albania.

There are few Americans in southern Albania, where most of the unrest has taken place. In the northern part of the country, there are about 1,600 Americans. Washington on Monday urged Americans to defer travel to Albania and said those now in the country should "observe the curfew, observe the laws, stay out of harm's way and seriously consider leaving if they feel their security situation is in any jeopardy."
Albania's government moved to regain control of towns in the south of the Balkan state on Tuesday after a weekend of armed unrest, as Berisha met the political opposition over the crisis.

Security forces with orders to shoot armed protesters on sight have been moving south from Tirana to quash violence since a state of emergency was declared by parliament on Sunday. The disorder erupted after a wave of protests, mainly in the south of Europe's poorest country, was sparked by the collapse in January of high-risk pyramid investment schemes.
